When two solids are pressed together they are not isolated from one another – the atoms at the surfaces can collide and share energy.  
That exchange of energy is what we call **heat transfer**.  

### 1. What temperature means  
For a solid, the temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the atoms that make up the material.  
* Hotter → the atoms, on average, move faster.  
* Colder → the atoms, on average, move more slowly.

### 2. Energy conservation in a closed pair  
If we look at the two objects together as a single closed system (no energy enters or leaves from outside), the total internal energy of the pair stays the same.  
When energy moves from one object to the other, one loses kinetic energy while the other gains it, but the sum does not change.

### 3. How the exchange proceeds  
* At the contact surface, atoms from the hotter body are, on average, moving faster than those from the cooler body.  
* When a fast atom collides with a slower one, it transfers a bit of its kinetic energy to the slower atom.  
* After many such collisions, the fast atoms become a little slower and the slow atoms become a little faster.

Because every collision works in this direction, **net heat always flows from the hotter object to the colder one**.  

### 4. When does the flow stop?  
The flow continues only while there is a difference in average kinetic energy—that is, while the temperatures are different.  
When the two bodies have the same average kinetic energy, collisions no longer produce a systematic transfer of energy; the energy that moves in one direction is, on average, balanced by the energy that moves the opposite way. At that point the **net heat flow is zero**, and the system is said to be in **thermal equilibrium**.

### 5. Why one object doesn’t keep getting hotter while the other keeps getting colder  
If one object tried to become hotter while the other became colder, a temperature difference would exist. That temperature difference itself creates a driving force for heat to move from the hot side to the cold side, exactly the opposite of what would be needed to maintain the difference. The only stable situation—where no net energy is forced to move—is the one where the temperatures are equal.

### Summary  
Two objects in contact exchange kinetic energy through countless microscopic collisions. Energy is conserved, so the hotter object loses some kinetic energy while the cooler one gains the same amount. This process continues until the average kinetic energies (and therefore the temperatures) are equal, at which point there is no longer a net flow of heat. That final state, where both objects share the same temperature, is called thermal equilibrium.

When we say the thermal energy has become *uniformly distributed*, we mean that every part of the system has, on average, the same amount of kinetic energy per particle. In everyday language that is the same as saying the whole system has one single temperature.

---

### 1.  What a closed system is

A **closed system** can exchange energy only *inside* itself; nothing (no heat, no work, no matter) can get in or out.  
If you put a hot metal ball into a container of cold water and seal the container, the metal‑water pair is a closed system. All the energy that moves around stays inside that container.

---

### 2.  How the energy moves – the microscopic picture  

* **Thermal energy = random motion of particles**.  
  In the hot part the atoms or molecules are moving fast; in the cold part they move more slowly.

* **Collisions are the messenger.**  
  When a fast particle from the hot region bumps into a slower particle from the cold region, part of its kinetic energy is transferred to the slower particle. After the collision both particles have intermediate speeds.

* **Many collisions, many particles.**  
  In a real material there are *astronomically* many particles (≈ 10²³ per gram). Each particle collides billions of times per second, constantly sharing its energy with neighbours.

* **The net result:**  
  Energy “spreads out” from the region where particles are, on average, fast (high temperature) to the region where they are slower (low temperature). The process continues until the average speed of particles is the same everywhere—i.e., the temperature is uniform.

---

### 3.  The macroscopic view – temperature equalizes  

From the point of view of a thermometer we see:

1. The hot object’s temperature drops.
2. The cold object’s temperature rises.
3. After some time the two temperatures meet in the middle and stay there.

Because no energy can leave the closed system, the total amount of thermal energy stays the same; it has only been **re‑arranged** among the particles.

---

### 4.  Why the uniform state is the “natural” one  

Statistically, there are vastly more ways for the particles to share a given amount of energy **evenly** than to keep it piled up in one part.  
Think of shuffling a deck of cards: there are many more possible orders where the red and black cards are mixed than where all reds are together.  
Similarly, the state with the same average kinetic energy everywhere (the same temperature) is the most probable state. The system “wants” to be in that state, which is why the energy flow stops only when uniformity is reached.

---

### 5.  Summary  

* When a hot and a cold object are placed together in a closed system, the fast‑moving particles of the hot side repeatedly collide with the slower particles of the cold side.  
* Each collision transfers a bit of kinetic energy, so the hot side cools and the cold side warms.  
* After countless collisions, the average kinetic energy per particle is the same everywhere; the temperature is uniform and the thermal energy is said to be uniformly distributed.  
* The total thermal energy is conserved (it stays inside the closed system); only its distribution changes, moving toward the most probable, highest‑entropy state.  

That is why, in everyday life, a cup of hot coffee left in a room eventually cools down to room temperature—the thermal energy has become uniformly spread throughout the coffee, the cup, the air, and the surroundings.

|--------|----------------|

When you pour hot water together with cold water, the two liquids will exchange heat until they reach a **common temperature**.  
The rule that governs this process is **conservation of energy**: the total amount of thermal energy (heat) in the system does not disappear; it is merely redistributed between the two parts.

---

### 1. What is “thermal energy” in water?
For a given mass \(m\) of water, the amount of heat it contains is

\[
Q = m \, c \, T ,
\]

where  

* \(c\) is the **specific heat capacity** of water (about \(4.18\ \text{J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹}\)), and  
* \(T\) is its temperature (in °C).

\(c\) tells us how much energy is needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C.

---

### 2. Mixing two portions

Suppose we have  

* \(m_h\) grams of hot water at temperature \(T_h\) (e.g., 80 °C) and  
* \(m_c\) grams of cold water at temperature \(T_c\) (e.g., 20 °C).

After mixing, the water reaches a single temperature \(T_f\).  
Because no heat is lost to the surroundings (we assume an insulated container), the heat lost by the hot water equals the heat gained by the cold water:

\[
\underbrace{m_h c (T_h - T_f)}_{\text{heat lost}} = \underbrace{m_c c (T_f - T_c)}_{\text{heat gained}} .
\]

The same specific‑heat \(c\) appears on both sides, so it cancels out. Solving for \(T_f\) gives

\[
T_f = \frac{m_h T_h + m_c T_c}{m_h + m_c}.
\]

---

### 3. Why the final temperature is *between* the two starts

The formula is a **weighted average** of the two original temperatures.  
*If the masses are equal* (\(m_h = m_c\)), the weights are the same and

\[
T_f = \frac{T_h + T_c}{2},
\]

the simple arithmetic mean—exactly halfway between the hot and cold temperatures.

If the hot water mass is larger, its temperature gets a larger weight, pulling \(T_f\) closer to \(T_h\); the opposite happens if the cold water mass is larger. In every case \(T_f\) lies **between** \(T_h\) and \(T_c\) because the average of two numbers can never be smaller than the smaller number or larger than the larger number.

---

### 4. A quick example

Take 200 g of water at 80 °C and 100 g at 20 °C.

\[
T_f = \frac{200 \times 80 + 100 \times 20}{200 + 100}
     = \frac{16000 + 2000}{300}
     = \frac{18000}{300}
     = 60^\circ\text{C}.
\]

The final temperature (60 °C) is indeed between 20 °C and 80 °C, and it is closer to the hotter water because there is more of it.

---

### 5. What would be needed to get a final temperature *outside* the original range?

Only if heat were added from or taken away by something else (e.g., the container losing heat to the air, a heater turning on, or an ice cube melting). In a closed, insulated mixture, the temperature must settle somewhere between the initial hot and cold values.

---

**In short:**  
Mixing hot and cold water causes heat to flow from the hotter part to the cooler part until both have the same temperature. The final temperature is a weighted average of the two starting temperatures, so it always ends up somewhere between them.

**Entropy and the “even‑ness’’ of energy**

In thermodynamics the word *entropy* is a measure of how many different microscopic ways a system can be arranged while still looking the same overall (same temperature, pressure, total energy, …).  
The more possible arrangements (called *microstates*), the higher the entropy.

---

### 1. Energy can be stored in many places  

Take a container of gas. The total internal energy \(U\) is the sum of the kinetic energy of all the molecules.  
If most of that energy is concentrated in a few fast‑moving molecules and the rest are slow, there are only a limited number of ways to pick which molecules are the fast ones.  

If the same total energy is shared **evenly** among all the molecules, every molecule can have a slightly different speed, and there are far more possible combinations of individual speeds that give the same overall energy. In statistical‑mechanics language:

\[
\text{Number of microstates } \Omega \propto \frac{U^{N}}{N!} \quad\text{(roughly)},
\]

where \(N\) is the number of particles. When the energy is spread uniformly, \(\Omega\) becomes much larger.

---

### 2. More microstates → higher entropy  

Entropy \(S\) is defined (Boltzmann) as  

\[
S = k_{\mathrm B}\,\ln \Omega ,
\]

where \(k_{\mathrm B}\) is Boltzmann’s constant and \(\Omega\) is the number of microstates.  
Because the natural logarithm is a monotonic function, a larger \(\Omega\) always means a larger \(S\).  

So, when the same amount of energy is redistributed more evenly, the number of ways to realize that distribution grows, and the entropy rises.

---

### 3. Everyday examples  

| Situation | Before | After | Why entropy is higher |
|-----------|--------|-------|-----------------------|
| Heat flows from a hot cup of coffee to a cool room | Energy concentrated in the coffee | Energy spread throughout the air | Many more molecular speed patterns in the whole room than just in the coffee |
| A gas expands into an empty chamber | Molecules confined to a small volume | Molecules fill the whole volume | Each molecule can now be in many more positions, giving many more microstates |
| Mixing two liquids (e.g., water and alcohol) | Molecules mostly surrounded by like molecules | Molecules intermingled | Vastly more ways to arrange the two kinds of molecules together |

In each case the total energy (or number of particles) hasn’t changed, but the way that energy is *distributed* becomes more uniform. That uniform distribution corresponds to many more microscopic possibilities, so the entropy increases.

---

### 4. The big picture – the Second Law  

The **Second Law of Thermodynamics** says that for an isolated system the entropy never decreases.  
Nature “prefers’’ the state that can be realized in the greatest number of ways.  
Even spreading of energy is just one manifestation of that preference: a uniform distribution gives the system the most freedom to arrange its particles, and therefore the highest entropy.

---

**In short:**  
When energy spreads out evenly, there are many more microscopic ways to achieve that same overall state. Because entropy counts those possibilities (via \(S = k_{\mathrm B}\ln \Omega\)), a more even energy distribution always means a higher entropy.
rationale: The candidate correctly explains that spreading energy uniformly increases the number of microscopic arrangements (microstates), leading to higher entropy, matching the reference answer.

**Entropy measures how many ways a system’s energy can be arranged.**  
When the same amount of energy can be put into a system in many different ways, the system is said to have a **high entropy**. When there are only a few possible arrangements, the entropy is low.

---

### 1. Energy and “micro‑states”

Imagine a box that contains a few tiny particles (atoms or molecules).  
Each particle can have a certain amount of kinetic energy and can be located
anywhere inside the box. A **micro‑state** is a complete description of every
particle’s position and its energy.  

If we count how many distinct micro‑states are compatible with the overall
energy we give the system, the larger that number, the larger the entropy.

Statistical physics gives the quantitative relation  

\[
S = k_{\!B}\,\ln W,
\]

where  

* \(S\) is the entropy,  
* \(k_{\!B}\) is Boltzmann’s constant (a tiny number that makes the units work), and  
* \(W\) is the number of possible micro‑states.

Because the natural logarithm grows when \(W\) grows, more possible
micro‑states → larger \(S\).

---

### 2. “Energy spreading out” = more micro‑states

Consider two simple situations.

| Situation | Energy distribution | How many micro‑states? |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------------------|
| **A** | All the energy is packed into a single, small region (a hot spot). | Very few ways to place that energy – it must stay in that region. |
| **B** | The same total energy is spread uniformly throughout the whole box. | Many ways: each tiny part of the box can hold a little bit of the energy, and the particles can exchange energy in countless combinations. |

In **A**, the energy is concentrated; there are only a handful of ways to
arrange the particles while keeping that concentration. In **B**, the same
total energy is divided among many parts of the system, so we can shuffle
tiny amounts of energy from place to place in countless ways. The number
\(W\) of allowed micro‑states is therefore much larger when the energy is
evenly spread.

Because \(S = k_{\!B}\ln W\), the entropy is higher in the evenly‑distributed
case.

---

### 3. Everyday example – a hot cup of coffee

A steaming cup of coffee placed in a cold room initially has the coffee’s
molecules moving fast (high kinetic energy) while the air molecules are
slow. The energy is **localized** in the coffee, so the total number of
micro‑states is relatively low.

Heat flows from the coffee to the surrounding air until the coffee and the
air reach the same temperature. Now the same total energy is shared among a
much larger number of molecules (both coffee and air). There are vastly more
ways to distribute that energy, so the entropy of the combined coffee‑plus‑air
system has increased.

---

### 4. Why the second law follows

Nature does not “choose” a low‑entropy arrangement; it simply moves toward the
states that are **most numerous** because random microscopic motions are
equally likely to go any way. Since the number of micro‑states is greatest
when energy is spread out as evenly as possible, the overall entropy tends to
increase. This is the statistical interpretation of the second law of
thermodynamics.

---

### Summary

* Entropy measures the number of microscopic ways a system can hold a given
  amount of energy.  
* When energy is concentrated, only a few arrangements are possible → low
  entropy.  
* When the same energy is spread out evenly, many more arrangements become
  possible → high entropy.  

Thus “energy spreading out more evenly” corresponds directly to an increase
in entropy.

**What happens when you mix hot and cold water?**  

When two amounts of water are poured together, the heat that the hotter water carries flows into the cooler water until the whole mixture reaches **thermal equilibrium** – a state where every part of the water has the same temperature.  

---

### 1. Energy can’t be created or destroyed  

The only thing that changes during mixing is how the **thermal energy** (the energy associated with temperature) is distributed.  
- The hot water starts with a lot of thermal energy.  
- The cold water starts with less thermal energy.  

When they touch, energy moves from the hot side to the cold side. The total amount of thermal energy in the combined water is just the sum of the energy that each portion had before they were mixed. No energy disappears (assuming we ignore heat lost to the surrounding air).

---

### 2. How we calculate the final temperature  

For water the **specific heat capacity** \(c\) – the amount of energy needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 °C – is essentially the same for every sample.  
If we mix  

* \(m_1\) kilograms of water at temperature \(T_1\) (hot) and  
* \(m_2\) kilograms of water at temperature \(T_2\) (cold),

the thermal energy each part carries is  

\[
Q_1 = m_1 c T_1,\qquad Q_2 = m_2 c T_2 .
\]

After mixing, the total mass is \(m_1+m_2\) and the mixture has a uniform temperature \(T_f\). Its energy is  

\[
Q_{\text{final}} = (m_1+m_2) c T_f .
\]

Because energy is conserved,

\[
m_1 c T_1 + m_2 c T_2 = (m_1+m_2) c T_f .
\]

The \(c\) cancels, giving the **weighted‑average formula**

\[
\boxed{\,T_f = \frac{m_1 T_1 + m_2 T_2}{m_1+m_2}\,}.
\]

---

### 3. Why the result must lie between the two starting temperatures  

The expression above is a **weighted average** of \(T_1\) and \(T_2\).  
*If both masses are positive (they are), the numerator is a sum of two numbers, each multiplied by a positive weight, and the denominator is the total of those weights.*  

A weighted average can never be larger than the largest number being averaged, nor smaller than the smallest. Consequently

\[
\min(T_1,T_2) \le T_f \le \max(T_1,T_2).
\]

So the final temperature is always somewhere between the hot and the cold starting temperatures.

---

### 4. A simple example  

Suppose you mix equal amounts of water:  

- 1 kg at \(80^\circ\text{C}\) (hot)  
- 1 kg at \(20^\circ\text{C}\) (cold)

Using the formula with \(m_1 = m_2\):

\[
T_f = \frac{1\cdot 80 + 1\cdot 20}{1+1} = \frac{100}{2} = 50^\circ\text{C}.
\]

The mixture is exactly the arithmetic mean because the masses are the same.  
If you used twice as much cold water (2 kg at \(20^\circ\text{C}\)) and 1 kg hot water, the result would be

\[
T_f = \frac{1\cdot 80 + 2\cdot 20}{1+2} = \frac{80+40}{3} \approx 40^\circ\text{C},
\]

still between 20 °C and 80 °C, but closer to the colder side because there is more cold water.

---

### 5. Real‑world notes  

* In an open sink some heat may escape to the air, making the final temperature a little lower than the ideal calculation.  
* If the water is not pure (e.g., contains salts) the specific heat changes slightly, but the same principle—energy conservation and weighted averaging—still holds.

---

**Bottom line:** Mixing hot and cold water spreads the thermal energy from the hotter part into the cooler part until the whole batch shares the same temperature. Because the total energy is just the sum of the two original amounts, the resulting temperature must sit between the two starting temperatures.
rationale: The candidate correctly explains energy conservation, derives the weighted‑average formula for final temperature, and shows why the result must lie between the initial temperatures, matching the reference answer.

\[
F = k \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^{2}}
\]

where

* \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) = the two charges,  
* \(r\) = the distance between the charges, and  
* \(k \approx 8.99 \times 10^{9}\,\text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2\) is a constant.

The key part of the formula is the \(1/r^{2}\) factor: the force varies **inversely with the square of the distance**.  

If the distance is **doubled**, the new distance is \(r' = 2r\). Plugging this into the formula:

\[
F' = k \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{(2r)^{2}} = k \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{4r^{2}} = \frac{1}{4}\, k \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^{2}} = \frac{F}{4}
\]

So the electric force becomes **one‑fourth** of its original value. In other words, doubling the separation reduces the force by a factor of 4. This is an example of an *inverse‑square law*, which also appears in gravity and light intensity.

   - The macrostate “energy all on the left” therefore has a small \(\Omega\) and low entropy.

3. **Energy spreading out = many more microstates**  
   When the wall is removed (or the system is allowed to exchange heat), the energetic molecules wander into the right side. After some time the energy is roughly evenly distributed between the two halves.  
   - Now many different sets of particle positions and speeds can give the same overall energy distribution (e.g., some fast molecules on the left, some on the right, etc.).  
   - The number of possible microstates \(\Omega\) is much larger, so the entropy rises.

4. **Why “evenness” matters**  
   An even spread of energy means that each small region of the system can have a wide range of possible energies without violating the overall constraints.  
   - If you try to keep energy clumped, you restrict the particles’ freedom: many configurations are forbidden, limiting \(\Omega\).  
   - When energy is uniform, each particle can be anywhere with many possible speeds, giving a combinatorial explosion of allowed arrangements.

   - **Mixing milk into coffee**: initially the coffee is hot (high energy) and the milk is cold (low energy). After stirring, the temperature becomes uniform. The mixed state can be achieved in countless ways (different molecules of milk and coffee swapping places), so its entropy is higher.

6. **Link to the Second Law**  
   The Second Law of Thermodynamics says that for an isolated system the entropy never decreases spontaneously. Because the uniform‑energy macrostate has the greatest \(\Omega\), natural processes tend to move toward that state: energy spreads out, and entropy rises.

---

**Bottom line:**  
When energy spreads out evenly, the system gains many more possible microscopic arrangements that look the same macroscopically. More possible arrangements mean a larger \(\Omega\), and since entropy is proportional to the logarithm of \(\Omega\), the entropy increases. **What a “closed system” means**

In physics we often draw an imaginary boundary around the part of the world we are studying.  
- **Open system** – material (mass) can cross the boundary.  
- **Closed system** – material cannot cross, but energy (heat, light, work) *can* cross.  
- **Isolated system** – neither mass nor energy can cross; it is completely sealed off.

When we talk about two objects that exchange thermal energy—say a hot metal rod placed in cold water—we usually treat the metal + water together as a **closed system**. The metal and the water stay inside the boundary, but heat can flow from one to the other.

---

### Why the closed‑system idea matters for heat transfer

1. **Conservation of energy inside the boundary**  
   The first law of thermodynamics (the “energy‑conservation law”) for a closed system is  

   \[
   \Delta U = Q - W
   \]

   where  
   \(\Delta U\) = change in the system’s internal energy,  
   \(Q\) = heat added to the system,  
   \(W\) = work done *by* the system on its surroundings.

   If no mechanical work is done (the objects just sit there), \(W = 0\) and the heat that leaves the hot object must equal the heat that enters the cold one:

   \[
   Q_{\text{hot}} + Q_{\text{cold}} = 0 .
   \]

   This relation lets us solve for the final temperature after the two objects come to equilibrium.

2. **No hidden mass‑energy flows**  
   Because mass can’t leave or enter, we don’t have to worry about things like steam escaping or cold air flowing in. All the energy change is contained in the objects we see, making the math much simpler.

3. **Defining the “system” correctly gives correct answers**  
   If we mistakenly treat the metal and water as separate *open* systems, we might think that the metal loses heat to “the surroundings” and the water gains heat from “the surroundings.” That double‑counts the same energy transfer and leads to wrong temperature predictions.

---

### A simple example

Suppose 100 g of water at 20 °C is placed in a 200 g piece of aluminum initially at 80 °C.  
We take the water + aluminum as a closed system (no mass leaves, no work done).  

Using the specific heat capacities  
- water: \(c_w = 4.18\ \text{J·g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)  
- aluminum: \(c_{Al} = 0.90\ \text{J·g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\),

the heat lost by the aluminum equals the heat gained by the water:

\[
m_{Al}c_{Al}(T_{i,Al}-T_f)=m_{w}c_{w}(T_f-T_{i,w}).
\]

Solving for the final temperature \(T_f\) (about 31 °C) works because we know **all** the energy stays inside our closed system. If the system were open—say, if some hot steam escaped—we would need extra terms to account for that loss.

---

### What changes if the system isn’t closed?

- **Open system**: Mass flows in or out (e.g., steam leaving the pot). Then the energy carried by that mass must be added to the heat balance, making calculations more complex.
- **Isolated system**: No heat can cross the boundary at all. The two objects would never exchange thermal energy, so their temperatures would stay the same forever—an idealization that helps us see the limits of real processes.

---

### Bottom line

Treating the hot and cold objects as a **closed system** tells us that:

- The total amount of thermal energy inside the boundary doesn’t disappear; it just moves from the hotter part to the cooler part.
- Because no material leaves or enters, we can set the heat lost by the hot side equal to the heat gained by the cold side and use that equality to find things like the final temperature or the amount of heat transferred.

That’s why the concept of a closed system is a fundamental bookkeeping tool when we study thermal energy transfer.

When we talk about two objects—a hot one and a cold one—most textbook problems treat them as a **closed system**. The only thing that can move in or out of the system is thermal energy (heat). The masses of the objects stay the same.

---

### Why the closed‑system idea matters for heat transfer

1. **Energy conservation is easy to apply**  
   The first law of thermodynamics (energy conservation) for a closed system says  

   \[
   \Delta U = Q - W ,
   \]

   where  
   \(\Delta U\) = change in internal energy of the system,  
   \(Q\) = heat added to the system,  
   \(W\) = work done by the system.

   In the simple case of two solids touching each other, there is essentially **no work** (\(W≈0\)). All the heat that leaves the hot object must enter the cold one, so

   \[
   Q_{\text{hot}} + Q_{\text{cold}} = 0 .
   \]

   This lets us write a single algebraic equation to find the final (equilibrium) temperature.

2. **We can use heat‑capacity formulas**  
   For each object we have  

   \[
   Q = mc\Delta T,
   \]

   where \(m\) is mass, \(c\) is specific heat capacity, and \(\Delta T\) is the temperature change.  
   Because the system is closed, the heat lost by the hot object (\(Q_{\text{hot}} = -m_hc_h\Delta T_h\)) is exactly the heat gained by the cold object (\(Q_{\text{cold}} = +m_c c_c \Delta T_c\)). Solving

   \[
   m_hc_h\Delta T_h = m_c c_c \Delta T_c
   \]

   gives the common final temperature. Without the closed‑system assumption we would have to account for heat that escaped to the air, a surrounding fluid, etc., which makes the math more complicated.

3. **No hidden mass‑transfer effects**  
   If the system were open, matter could leave or enter (think of steam escaping from a boiling kettle). When mass leaves, it carries internal energy with it, and the simple “heat lost = heat gained” rule no longer holds. You would have to track both mass flow and its associated energy, which is beyond the scope of most introductory thermal‑energy problems.

4. **Helps illustrate the second law**  
   In a closed system the total entropy (a measure of disorder) must increase when heat flows from hot to cold. Because no mass or extra energy is coming in, we can focus purely on the entropy change due to the temperature difference:

   \[
   \Delta S_{\text{total}} = \frac{Q_{\text{cold}}}{T_{\text{cold}}} - \frac{Q_{\text{hot}}}{T_{\text{hot}}} \ge 0 .
   \]

   This clean picture would be muddied if extra energy were entering or leaving the system.

---

### What happens if the system isn’t closed?

| Situation | What changes? |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Open system (e.g., boiling water with steam escaping)** | Heat leaves with the steam, so the remaining water cools faster than predicted by the simple closed‑system equation. You must add a term for the energy carried away by the escaping mass. |
| **Isolated system (perfect insulation)** | No heat leaves at all; the only energy exchange is between the two objects. The final temperature can be found exactly with the closed‑system equation, and the total entropy increase is the smallest possible. |

---

### Bottom line

Treating the hot and cold objects as a **closed system** lets us:

* Apply the conservation of energy without worrying about mass flow.  
* Use the simple relation “heat lost = heat gained” to calculate temperature changes.  
* Keep the analysis focused on thermal energy alone, making it possible to see clearly how heat moves and why it always goes from hot to cold.

When the system isn’t closed, extra terms for mass and energy exchange must be added, which complicates the problem and changes the final temperature and entropy outcomes. In most introductory physics and chemistry problems, assuming a closed system is the reason we can solve the heat‑transfer question with only a few equations.

### What a “closed system” means

In physics we think of a **system** as the part of the world we want to study, and we draw an imaginary surface around it (the “boundary”).  
A **closed system** has one special rule:

*Mass cannot cross the boundary, but energy (heat, work, radiation) can.*

So no material leaves or enters, but heat can flow in or out, and the system can do work on its surroundings or have work done on it.

---

### Why the definition matters for heat transfer

1. **Energy can’t disappear – it just moves.**  
   The first law of thermodynamics (the law of energy conservation) says  

   \[
   \Delta U = Q - W
   \]

   where  

   * \(\Delta U\) = change in the system’s internal energy,  
   * \(Q\) = heat added to the system,  
   * \(W\) = work done by the system on its surroundings.  

   When we know the system is closed, we are allowed to use this equation because we know no hidden mass is bringing extra energy in or taking it away.

2. **We can count all the heat that moves.**  
   Imagine a hot metal block placed in a cold water bath. If we treat the **block + water** together as a closed system, the only way the internal energy can change is by heat flowing from the block to the water (and possibly a tiny amount of work due to expansion). No mass is leaving, so the total amount of energy lost by the block must equal the energy gained by the water.

3. **It tells us how fast the temperatures will equalize.**  
   The rate at which heat moves depends on the temperature difference and on the properties of the materials (thermal conductivity, surface area, etc.). In a closed system we can write a simple balance:

   \[
   \text{heat lost by hot object} = \text{heat gained by cold object}
   \]

   If we mistakenly treated the system as “open” (allowing mass to leave), we would have to add extra terms for the energy carried away by that mass, making the analysis much more complicated.

4. **It lets us define the “surroundings.”**  
   By drawing the boundary, we decide what counts as the system and what counts as the surroundings. In the metal‑block‑in‑water example, we could choose the block alone as the system. Then the water is the surroundings, and the heat that leaves the block is **\(Q_{\text{out}}\)**. The first‑law equation for the block alone becomes  

   \[
   \Delta U_{\text{block}} = -Q_{\text{out}}
   \]

   (no work term if the block doesn’t move). Choosing the block + water together as the system makes the heat flow internal to the system, so \(Q_{\text{out}} = 0\) for the combined system, and the only change is the redistribution of internal energy.

---

### Real‑world examples

| Situation | Reasonable closed‑system choice | What we learn |
|-----------|--------------------------------|----------------|
| A cup of hot coffee cooling on a table | Cup + air around it (no steam escaping) | Total energy lost by coffee = energy gained by surrounding air + small loss by radiation. |
| A sealed can of soup heated on a stove | The soup *inside* the can (no soup leaves) | Heat from the stove goes into the soup; we can calculate the temperature rise using \(Q = mc\Delta T\). |
| Ice melting in a bowl of water (bowl not covered) | Ice + water + bowl (mass stays, water may splash out) | If water splashes, the system is no longer closed; we must include the energy carried away by the spilled water. |

---

### Bottom line

Treating the hot and cold objects (and any material that stays with them) as a **closed system** gives us a clean bookkeeping tool:

* The **total energy** inside the boundary stays constant (aside from work or heat crossing the boundary).  
* All the heat that leaves the hot part must appear somewhere else inside the boundary.  
* We can apply the simple equation \(\Delta U = Q - W\) without extra terms for mass flow.

Because of these points, the concept of a closed system is essential for correctly predicting how, why, and how fast thermal energy moves from a hotter object to a colder one.

### Pulling the charges apart

**Electric potential energy of two point charges**

For two point charges \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) separated by a distance \(r\), the electric potential energy \(U\) of the pair is  

\[
U = \frac{k\,q_1 q_2}{r},
\]

where  

* \(k = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\approx 9.0\times10^{9}\ \text{N·m}^2\!/\!\text{C}^2\) is Coulomb’s constant,  
* \(r\) is the separation between the charges.

The sign of \(U\) depends on the signs of the charges:

* **Like charges** (\(q_1 q_2 > 0\)) → \(U\) is **positive**.  
* **Opposite charges** (\(q_1 q_2 < 0\)) → \(U\) is **negative**.

A negative potential energy means that the two charges are in a **bound** (attractive) state; they would release energy if they were allowed to come together.

---

### Pulling opposite charges farther apart

Suppose we have an opposite‑charge pair, e.g. \(q_1 = +q\) and \(q_2 = -q\). Their potential energy is

\[
U(r) = \frac{k(+q)(-q)}{r}= -\,\frac{k q^{2}}{r}.
\]

Here \(U\) is **negative** and its magnitude \(|U| = \dfrac{k q^{2}}{r}\) gets larger as \(r\) gets smaller.

If an external agent (your hand, a mechanical device, etc.) pulls the charges **farther apart**, the distance \(r\) increases. Look at the formula:

\[
U(r) = -\frac{k q^{2}}{r}.
\]

* As \(r\) becomes larger, the denominator grows, so the fraction \(\frac{k q^{2}}{r}\) becomes **smaller**.
* Because of the minus sign, the value of \(U\) becomes **less negative** (it moves toward zero).

In other words, the potential energy **increases** (it climbs upward from a large negative value toward zero).  

Mathematically, the change in potential energy when the separation changes from \(r_1\) to \(r_2\) is

\[
\Delta U = U(r_2)-U(r_1) = -\frac{k q^{2}}{r_2}+ \frac{k q^{2}}{r_1}
        = k q^{2}\!\left(\frac{1}{r_1}-\frac{1}{r_2}\right).
\]

Since \(r_2 > r_1\), the term \(\frac{1}{r_2}\) is smaller than \(\frac{1}{r_1}\), making \(\Delta U\) **positive**.

---

### Where does the extra energy come from?

The external force you apply must **do work against the attractive electric force** between the charges. The work you do on the system is exactly the increase in its electric potential energy:

\[
\text{Work done by external agent} = \Delta U \; (>0).
\]

If you later let the charges go back together, the electric attraction will do positive work on them, and the stored potential energy will be released (for example, as kinetic energy or heat).

---

### Summary

* Two opposite charges have **negative** electric potential energy \(-k q^{2}/r\).
* Pulling them farther apart **increases** that energy (makes it less negative) because the magnitude \(|U| = k q^{2}/r\) decreases with distance.
* The increase in energy comes from the **work** you do with an external force against the attractive electric force.
rationale: The candidate correctly explains that pulling opposite charges apart increases the system's electric potential energy, requiring work done against the attractive force, which matches the reference answer.

**What is happening when we pull two like charges together?**

1. **Like charges repel**  
   A positive charge creates an electric field that pushes other positive charges away (and a negative charge pushes other negatives away). The force between two point charges \(q_{1}\) and \(q_{2}\) is given by Coulomb’s law  

   \[
   F = k\frac{|q_{1}q_{2}|}{r^{2}},
   \]

   where  

   * \(k = 8.99\times10^{9}\ \text{N·m}^{2}\!/\text{C}^{2}\) (Coulomb’s constant),  
   * \(r\) is the distance between the charges, and  
   * the force is **repulsive** because the charges have the same sign.

2. **Work must be done against the repulsive force**  
   To bring the charges from a large separation to a smaller one, you have to push them **against** this repulsion. Doing that requires you to supply energy. In physics “work” is the energy transferred when a force moves something through a distance:

   \[
   W = \int_{r_i}^{r_f} F\,dr .
   \]

3. **The force grows as the charges get closer**  
   Notice the \(1/r^{2}\) dependence in Coulomb’s law. As the distance \(r\) decreases, the force becomes larger very quickly. For example, halving the distance makes the force four times larger.

4. **Resulting electric potential energy**  
   The energy stored in the pair of charges is called *electric potential energy* \(U\). Carrying out the integral above gives

   \[
   U(r) = k\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r} .
   \]

   Because the charges are alike, \(q_{1}q_{2}>0\) and \(U\) is **positive**.  
   - At a moderate separation \(r_{\text{mid}}\) the energy is \(U_{\text{mid}} = k\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r_{\text{mid}}}\).  
   - At a much smaller separation \(r_{\text{close}}\) the energy is \(U_{\text{close}} = k\frac{q_{1}q_{2}}{r_{\text{close}}}\).

   Since \(r_{\text{close}} < r_{\text{mid}}\),

   \[
   U_{\text{close}} = \frac{r_{\text{mid}}}{r_{\text{close}}}\;U_{\text{mid}} \;>\;U_{\text{mid}} .
   \]

   The closer the charges, the larger the denominator in the formula becomes smaller, so the fraction—and therefore the stored energy—gets larger.

5. **Why more energy is required**  
   • **Stronger repulsion**: As they approach, the repulsive force rises sharply (∝ 1/r²).  
   • **More work against that force**: To move a charge an extra tiny distance when the force is already large, you must do more work.  
   • **Higher potential energy**: The system ends up with a larger amount of stored electric potential energy, which is exactly the work you supplied.

**Analogy:** Think of lifting a weight against gravity. Near the Earth’s surface the weight feels a constant force, so lifting it a certain height always needs the same amount of energy per meter. With electric charges, the “force per meter” gets bigger the closer you get, just like trying to compress a spring: the more you compress, the harder it pushes back, so you must put in more and more energy for each additional bit of compression.

**Bottom line:** Because the repulsive electric force grows rapidly as the distance shrinks, you must do increasingly more work (supply more energy) to bring two like charges from a moderate distance to a very close one. That extra work shows up as a larger electric potential energy of the charge pair.
rationale: The candidate correctly explains that the repulsive force between like charges grows as 1/r², requiring more work to reduce separation, which matches the reference answer.

**The repulsive force gets stronger as the charges get closer**

Two objects that have the same sign of electric charge (both positive or both negative) push each other away.  
The size of that push is given by **Coulomb’s law**

\[
F = k\,\frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^{2}},
\]

where  

* \(F\) = force on each charge,  
* \(q_1 , q_2\) = the amounts of charge,  
* \(r\) = distance between the charges, and  
* \(k \approx 8.99\times10^{9}\,\text{N·m}^{2}\!/\!\text{C}^{2}\) is a constant.

Notice the \(1/r^{2}\) dependence: **when the distance \(r\) is halved, the force becomes four times larger**.  
So as the charges are brought from a “moderate” separation to a very small one, the repulsive force they exert on each other grows dramatically.

---

### Work (energy) needed to bring them together

To move one charge toward the other you must **do work against that repulsive force**.  
If you push a charge a tiny distance \(dr\) while the force at that point is \(F(r)\), the little amount of work you do is

\[
dW = F(r)\,dr .
\]

To find the total work required to bring the charges from an initial distance \(r_i\) to a final distance \(r_f\) we add up (integrate) all those little contributions:

\[
W = \int_{r_i}^{r_f} F(r)\,dr
   = \int_{r_i}^{r_f} k\,\frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^{2}}\,dr
   = k\,|q_1 q_2|\left[\,-\frac{1}{r}\,\right]_{r_i}^{r_f}
   = k\,|q_1 q_2|\left(\frac{1}{r_f}-\frac{1}{r_i}\right).
\]

Because the charges are alike, \(q_1 q_2 > 0\) and the work \(W\) is **positive**—you have to put energy into the system.

If the final distance \(r_f\) is much smaller than the starting distance \(r_i\), the term \(1/r_f\) becomes large. That makes the whole expression for \(W\) larger, meaning **more energy must be supplied**.

---

### Electric potential energy picture

The same result is often written as the electric **potential energy** of two point charges:

\[
U(r)=k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}.
\]

For like charges \(q_1 q_2\) is positive, so \(U\) is a positive number that **increases as \(r\) gets smaller**. The change in potential energy \(\Delta U = U(r_f)-U(r_i)\) is exactly the work you had to do.

---

### Intuitive analogy

Think of two springs that push outward when you try to compress them. The further you compress the spring, the harder you have to push, and the more energy you store in the spring. Electric repulsion works the same way: the “spring constant” gets larger the closer the charges are, so squeezing them together (reducing \(r\)) requires ever‑greater effort.

---

**In short:** The electric repulsive force grows as the distance shrinks (\(F \propto 1/r^{2}\)). Because work is the force times the distance you move against it, the total work (or energy) you must supply to bring two like charges close together rises sharply as the final separation becomes small. This is why it takes much more energy to bring them very close than to keep them at a moderate distance.

**Magnetic dipole – external field**

A bar magnet can be treated as a **magnetic dipole**.  
The dipole has a vector **μ** (the magnetic dipole moment) that points from its south‑pole to its north‑pole.  
An external magnetic field is represented by the vector **B**.

---

### Potential energy of a magnetic dipole

The magnetic potential energy **U** of a dipole in a uniform external field is  

\[
U = -\,\mathbf{\mu}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{B}= -\mu B\cos\theta .
\]

* **\(\mu = |\mathbf{\mu}|\)** – strength of the magnet’s dipole moment.  
* **\(B = |\mathbf{B}|\)** – strength of the external field.  
* **\(\theta\)** – the angle between the two vectors (the angle between the magnet’s north‑south line and the direction of the field).

Because of the cosine term, **U depends only on the orientation** of the magnet relative to the field.

---

### What the formula tells us

| Orientation (θ) | \(\cos\theta\) | **U = –μB cosθ** | Energy description |
|-----------------|---------------|-------------------|--------------------|
| **θ = 0°** (magnet’s north pole points **with** the field) | +1 | **U = –μB** (most negative) | **Lowest possible energy** – stable equilibrium. |
| **θ = 90°** (magnet side‑on to the field) | 0 | **U = 0** | Midpoint; the magnet feels a torque but no net “push” toward higher or lower energy. |
| **θ = 180°** (north pole points **against** the field) | –1 | **U = +μB** (most positive) | **Highest possible energy** – unstable equilibrium. |

- **Minimum energy (θ = 0°):** The dipole aligns **parallel** to the field. This is the configuration the system “prefers” because it requires the least energy.
- **Maximum energy (θ = 180°):** The dipole is **anti‑parallel** to the field. A small disturbance will make it rotate away from this orientation because it can lower its energy.

---

### Why does the magnet rotate?

The torque on a magnetic dipole is

\[
\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{\mu} \times \mathbf{B}.
\]

The torque is zero when \(\theta = 0^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\) (vectors are parallel or anti‑parallel).  
For any other angle the cross‑product is non‑zero, producing a turning force that **tries to reduce \(\theta\)**, i.e., to bring the magnet into the lowest‑energy alignment.

---

### Everyday picture

Imagine a compass needle in Earth’s magnetic field.  
- When the needle points north (aligned with the field), it stays still—that’s the **low‑energy, stable** orientation.  
- If you try to flip it so the north end points south, you must do work against the field; the needle would snap back once released because that reversed position is **high‑energy, unstable**.

---

### Summary

- The potential energy of a bar magnet in an external uniform magnetic field is \(U = -\mu B \cos\theta\).
- **Energy is lowest** when the magnet’s north‑south axis is **parallel** to the field (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)).
- **Energy is highest** when the axis is **anti‑parallel** (\(\theta = 180^\circ\)).
- The magnet experiences a torque that tries to rotate it toward the low‑energy (parallel) orientation.

So, the orientation of the magnet directly controls its magnetic potential energy, and a free magnet will rotate until it reaches the orientation of minimum energy.

**Magnetic dipole and potential energy**

A bar magnet can be thought of as a tiny magnetic “arrow” called a **magnetic dipole**.  
It has a direction – from its South pole toward its North pole – and a strength, called the **magnetic dipole moment** (**μ**).  

When the magnet is placed in an external magnetic field (**B**), the two interact.  
The amount of energy stored in that interaction is the **magnetic potential energy** \(U\).

---

### The formula

For a dipole in a uniform field the potential energy is  

\[
\boxed{U = -\,\boldsymbol{\mu}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{B}= -\mu B\cos\theta}
\]

* \(\mu = |\boldsymbol{\mu}|\) – magnitude (strength) of the magnet’s dipole moment.  
* \(B = |\mathbf{B}|\) – magnitude of the external field.  
* \(\theta\) – the angle between the direction of the dipole moment (the magnet’s north‑to‑south line) and the direction of the field.  
* The dot product (\(\cdot\)) gives the product of the magnitudes times the cosine of the angle.

---

### How orientation changes the energy

| Angle \(\theta\) | \(\cos\theta\) | Potential energy \(U\) | What the magnet “wants” to do |
|------------------|---------------|-----------------------|--------------------------------|
| \(0^\circ\) (pointing **with** the field) | \(+1\) | \(U = -\mu B\) (most negative) | This is the **lowest‑energy** (stable) orientation. |
| \(90^\circ\) (perpendicular) | \(0\) | \(U = 0\) | No torque; the magnet can stay, but it’s a higher‑energy state than \(\theta=0\). |
| \(180^\circ\) (pointing **against** the field) | \(-1\) | \(U = +\mu B\) (most positive) | This is the **highest‑energy** (unstable) orientation. |

*Because the energy is negative when \(\cos\theta\) is positive, the system “prefers” to have the smallest (most negative) value of \(U\).*  

---

### Why does the magnet move?

The magnetic field exerts a **torque** on the dipole:

\[
\boldsymbol{\tau} = \boldsymbol{\mu}\times\mathbf{B}
\]

The torque is zero when \(\theta = 0^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\); otherwise it tries to rotate the magnet so that \(\theta\) decreases (i.e., the north pole turns toward the direction of the field). This rotation reduces the potential energy, just as a ball rolls downhill to lower its gravitational potential energy.

---

### Summary

* The potential energy of a bar magnet in an external uniform magnetic field depends on the cosine of the angle between the magnet’s dipole moment and the field: \(U = -\mu B\cos\theta\).  
* **Aligned** with the field (\(\theta = 0^\circ\)) gives the *lowest* (most negative) energy – a stable equilibrium.  
* **Opposite** to the field (\(\theta = 180^\circ\)) gives the *highest* energy – an unstable equilibrium.  
* At intermediate angles the energy lies between these two extremes, and the magnetic torque works to rotate the magnet toward the low‑energy, aligned position.

So, by simply turning the magnet, you change \(\theta\) and therefore change its magnetic potential energy.

**1. What a magnet really does**

A magnet creates a region around it called a **magnetic field**.  
The field is invisible, but at every point in space it has a direction (the direction a tiny compass needle would point) and a strength.  

When another magnet is placed in that field, the field exerts a force on it. The force can push the magnets apart (repel) or pull them together (attract) depending on how the north‑south poles are oriented.

**2. Force without contact**

The force does not need the magnets to touch because the magnetic field fills the space between them.  
Think of the field as a kind of “rope” that stretches from one magnet to the other. If the rope is stretched (like when the magnets are apart) it can pull the magnets together; if the rope is twisted (like opposite poles facing each other) it can push them apart. The rope is the field, and the pull or push is the magnetic force.  

This is similar to how the Earth’s gravity pulls a falling apple toward the ground even though the apple never touches the Earth before it lands.

**3. Where does the energy come from?**

Energy is not created out of nothing; it is stored in the magnetic field itself.  

* **Potential energy of the field** – When two magnets are held apart, the field lines are stretched and distorted, which requires energy. That energy is “potential energy” stored in the field, just like a stretched spring stores elastic potential energy.  

* **Doing work** – If the magnets are allowed to move, the magnetic force can cause them to accelerate. The stored potential energy is converted into **kinetic energy** (the energy of motion). Conversely, if you push the magnets together against a repelling force, you have to do work on the system; you are putting energy into the field, increasing its stored potential energy.

**4. How energy is transferred**

Consider two magnets that attract:

1. **Initial state** – The magnets are held apart. The magnetic field between them is stretched, storing some potential energy.  
2. **Release** – The attractive force pulls the magnets together. As they move, the field “relaxes,” and the stored potential energy is released.  
3. **Result** – The magnets speed up; the lost potential energy has become kinetic energy of the moving magnets. The energy has traveled from the field (where it was stored) to the magnets (where it appears as motion).

If you later stop the magnets (e.g., by catching them with a hand), the kinetic energy is transferred to you as heat or the motion of your hand. The magnetic field itself never “uses up” energy; it simply converts the form of energy that is already present.

**5. Summing up**

- Magnets act on each other through their magnetic fields, which extend through space, so no physical contact is needed.  
- The magnetic field can store energy, much like a compressed spring.  
- When the magnets move, the field’s stored energy changes form, transferring energy to (or from) the magnets.  

Thus, attraction or repulsion without contact is possible because the invisible magnetic field carries the force, and that same field can hold and exchange energy just like any other physical system.

### The magnetic field is the “medium” that lets magnets feel each other

When a magnet is placed in space it creates an **invisible magnetic field** around it.  
You can picture the field as a dense set of lines that start at the north pole of the magnet and end at its south pole.  
Anything that also carries a magnetic field (another magnet, a piece of iron, a coil of wire, …) feels the influence of those lines even if the objects never touch.

Because the field extends through the air, it can push or pull on another magnet that enters the region where the field is strong.  
That is why two magnets can **attract** (north‑south) or **repel** (north‑north or south‑south) without any physical contact.

---

## How energy gets transferred

1. **Magnetic force can do work**  
   Force × distance = work.  
   The magnetic field exerts a force on the other magnet, and if that magnet moves, the field does work on it.  
   - When opposite poles approach, the magnetic force pulls them together, speeding them up. The kinetic energy they gain comes from the magnetic field’s stored energy.  
   - When like poles push each other apart, the field does negative work (it takes kinetic energy away) and the magnets slow down.

2. **Energy is stored in the field itself**  
   A magnetic field contains energy. The energy density (energy per unit volume) is  

   \[
   u = \frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_0}
   \]

   where \(B\) is the magnetic‑field strength and \(\mu_0\) is a constant of free space.  
   When the magnets are far apart the field lines are spread out, and the stored energy is relatively high. When they come together, the pattern of the field changes and the total stored energy drops. The “missing” energy appears as kinetic energy of the moving magnets, heat, sound, etc.

3. **Changing fields can induce currents (another way to move energy)**  
   If the magnetic field through a loop of wire changes, an electric current is created (Faraday’s law). That current can power a device, so the moving magnet can transfer energy to electrical energy without ever touching the coil.

---

### Putting it together with a simple example

Imagine two bar magnets with opposite poles facing each other, held a few centimeters apart.

- **Step 1 – Release them:** The magnetic field pulls them together. No contact is needed; the field’s force does the pulling.
- **Step 2 – They move:** As they slide toward each other, the field does positive work on each magnet. Their speeds increase, so they now have kinetic energy.
- **Step 3 – Energy source:** The extra kinetic energy did not appear from nowhere; it came from the *magnetic potential energy* stored in the field. When the magnets finally touch, the field pattern is different and the stored energy is lower.

If instead the magnets were like‑poles and you pushed one toward the other, the field would resist the motion. You would have to do work (exert a force) to compress the magnetic “spring.” That work would be stored as extra magnetic potential energy, ready to be released later when the magnets are let go.

---

### Key take‑aways

- **Magnetic fields extend through space**, allowing forces to act at a distance.
- **A force that moves an object does work**, converting energy between the magnet’s kinetic energy and the energy stored in the magnetic field.
- The field itself **contains energy** (proportional to \(B^{2}\)). Changing the field configuration (by moving the magnets) moves that energy from the field to the magnets, or vice‑versa.
- Thus, magnets can attract or repel without touching **and still transfer energy**, exactly the way gravity can pull a falling apple or a spring can push a toy car—through a field that stores and releases energy.

**What a magnet does**

A magnet creates a **magnetic field** – an invisible “force field’’ that fills the space around it.  
Inside the field, a tiny magnetic dipole (the north‑south pair inside every piece of magnet) feels a force:

\[
\mathbf F = \nabla (\mathbf m\!\cdot\!\mathbf B)
\]

where  

* \(\mathbf m\) is the magnetic dipole moment of the magnet (a vector that points from its south pole to its north pole), and  
* \(\mathbf B\) is the magnetic field produced by the other magnet.

Because the field extends through empty space, the two magnets feel each other’s force **without touching**. That is why they can pull together or push apart at a distance.

---

### Where does the energy come from?

A magnetic field is not just a way to “talk’’ between the magnets; it **stores energy**.  
The energy contained in a magnetic field in a region of space is

\[
U = \frac{1}{2\mu_0}\int B^{2}\,dV ,
\]

where \(\mu_0\) is a constant and the integral runs over all space where the field exists.  
When the relative positions of the magnets change, the shape of the field changes, so the amount of stored energy changes.

*If the field energy decreases*, that lost energy appears as kinetic energy of the magnets – they speed up as they attract or as they are forced apart.  
*If the field energy increases* (for example, you push two like poles together), you must do work on the system; the extra energy is stored in the more “compressed’’ field.

Thus the **energy transfer** is really a reshaping of the magnetic field’s stored energy, not a flow of material from one magnet to the other.

---

### How can the field do work without contact?

Think of the field as a stretched rubber sheet that fills the space between the magnets.  
When you let the sheet relax (magnets attract), the sheet pulls the magnets together and the magnets move – mechanical work is done.  
When you pull the magnets apart, you have to stretch the sheet, doing work on it and storing more energy.

Because the field exists everywhere in space, the “pull’’ or “push’’ is transmitted instantly through that sheet, so the magnets never need to touch.

---

### Real‑world examples

* **Magnetic levitation (maglev) trains** – magnets in the train and the track repel each other, keeping the train suspended without contact. The magnetic field supplies the upward force and stores the energy that keeps the train aloft.
* **Magnetic brakes** – a moving metal plate passes near a strong magnet. The changing magnetic field induces electric currents in the metal, which create their own magnetic field that opposes the motion. Mechanical energy of the moving plate is transferred to the magnetic field and then turned into heat in the metal.
* **Electric generators** – a coil of wire is rotated in a magnetic field. The moving coil cuts magnetic field lines, producing an electric current; the mechanical energy of rotation is transferred to electrical energy via the field.

---

### Bottom line

Two magnets can attract or repel without touching because each creates a magnetic field that fills the space around it.  
The field carries energy; when the magnets move, the field’s configuration changes, and the corresponding change in field energy shows up as mechanical work on the magnets (or on anything else placed in the field).  
So the “transfer of energy’’ is really the field’s stored energy being redistributed, not a material thing passing from one magnet to the other.

**What “mechanical energy” means**

In a book‑Earth system the mechanical energy is the sum of  

* **Gravitational potential energy (U)** – the energy the book has because of its height above the Earth, and  

* **Kinetic energy (K)** – the energy it has because it is moving.

\(E_{\text{mech}} = K + U\)

(When we talk about the Earth too, the potential energy is really the energy of the Earth‑book pair, but we write it with the familiar formulas \(U = mgh\) or \(U = -\dfrac{GM_{\!E}m}{r}\).)

---

### 1. While the book is falling (free‑fall)

*The only force doing work on the book is gravity, which is a **conservative** force.*  
That means gravity can convert one form of mechanical energy into the other, but it does **not** create or destroy mechanical energy.

* As the book drops, its height \(h\) gets smaller → the gravitational potential energy \(U = mgh\) gets smaller.
* The loss of potential energy shows up as an equal gain in kinetic energy:  

\[
\Delta K = -\;\Delta U
\]

*The total mechanical energy \(E_{\text{mech}}\) stays the same throughout the fall (neglecting air resistance).*

So, during the fall the distribution shifts:

| Height | Potential Energy \(U\) | Kinetic Energy \(K\) |
|--------|-----------------------|----------------------|
| Top (just released) | Max (largest \(h\)) | 0 |
| Mid‑way | Decreases | Increases |
| Just before hitting the floor | Smallest (almost zero) | Largest (maximum speed) |

---

### 2. When the book hits the floor

The floor exerts a **non‑conservative** contact force. The book’s kinetic energy is rapidly turned into other forms:

* heat in the book and floor,
* sound,
* a tiny deformation of the floor and book (elastic potential energy that mostly becomes heat).

Because this energy is transferred to internal (thermal) energy, it is **no longer counted as mechanical energy** of the book‑Earth system. Therefore the mechanical energy **decreases** at the moment of impact.

---

### Summary

* **During free fall:** total mechanical energy of the book‑Earth system remains constant; gravitational potential energy drops while kinetic energy rises by the same amount.
* **At the impact:** kinetic energy is converted into heat, sound, etc., so the mechanical energy of the system is reduced (the lost mechanical energy appears as internal energy of the book, floor, and surrounding air).

response:
**What the system is**

When we talk about “the book‑Earth system” we treat the book and the Earth as one isolated pair.  
The only force that matters for the fall is the **gravitational force**, which is a **conservative** force (it does not dissipate energy). Because there is no appreciable air resistance or other friction, the mechanical energy of this pair is conserved.

---

### 1.  Total mechanical energy

Mechanical energy = kinetic energy (K) + gravitational potential energy (U).

If the book starts at rest on a shelf of height \(h\),

\[
K_{\text{initial}} = 0 ,\qquad 
U_{\text{initial}} = m g h .
\]

Just before it hits the floor (take the floor as the zero‑height reference),

\[
U_{\text{final}} = 0 ,\qquad 
K_{\text{final}} = \frac12 m v^{2}.
\]

Because the gravitational force is conservative,

\[
K_{\text{initial}}+U_{\text{initial}} = K_{\text{final}}+U_{\text{final}} .
\]

So the **total mechanical energy of the book‑Earth system stays the same** (to an excellent approximation).  
(The Earth actually acquires an infinitesimally tiny opposite momentum, but its kinetic energy is utterly negligible compared with that of the book.)

---

### 2.  How the energy is shared during the fall

| Moment | Height (h) | Potential Energy \(U = mgh\) | Kinetic Energy \(K = \frac12 mv^2\) | Total |
|--------|------------|------------------------------|------------------------------------|-------|
| At the shelf (start) | \(h_{\text{max}}\) | maximum (largest) | 0 (book at rest) | constant |
| Halfway down | \(h_{\text{max}}/2\) | half of the initial value | half of the initial value (because the lost PE becomes KE) | constant |
| Just before impact | 0 | 0 (reference level) | all the initial PE is now KE | constant |

Mathematically, for any point during the fall

\[
\Delta U = -\,m g\,\Delta h \quad (\text{negative, because }h\text{ decreases}),
\]
\[
\Delta K = +\,m g\,\Delta h \quad (\text{positive, same magnitude}).
\]

Thus **the decrease in gravitational potential energy is exactly matched by the increase in kinetic energy**.

---

### 3.  What happens at the instant of impact?

*If the collision were perfectly elastic* (the book bounces without losing energy), the kinetic energy would be converted back into potential energy as the book rises again, and the total mechanical energy would still be conserved.

*In the real world the impact is inelastic.*  
When the book hits the floor, some of its kinetic energy is transferred to other forms: heat, sound, deformation of the floor and the book, etc. That energy is no longer part of the mechanical energy of the book‑Earth pair, so the **mechanical energy of the pair decreases**, while the **total energy (mechanical + internal) of the whole universe stays constant**, as required by the law of energy conservation.

---

### Summary

- **Total mechanical energy of the isolated book‑Earth system is conserved during the free fall** (assuming negligible air resistance).  
- As the book drops, **gravitational potential energy steadily decreases** while **kinetic energy rises by the same amount**.  
- At the moment of impact, if energy is lost to heat, sound, etc., the mechanical energy of the book‑Earth system drops, but the lost mechanical energy is transformed into internal energy, keeping the overall energy of the universe unchanged.
rationale: The candidate correctly states that the mechanical energy of the book‑Earth system is conserved during the fall, with potential energy decreasing and kinetic energy increasing by the same amount, matching the reference answer.

|-------|------------------------|----------------------|--------------------------|

When the gas is trapped in a cylinder, its molecules are moving rapidly in all directions.  
Each molecule collides with the walls of the cylinder (including the piston) and bounces back.  
During a collision the molecule’s momentum changes, and by Newton’s 3rd law the wall feels an equal and opposite impulse.  

### From many collisions to a pressure

If you count the many tiny impulses that occur every second on the piston surface, you obtain a **force** \(F\).  
Dividing that force by the piston’s area \(A\) gives the **pressure** \(P\):

\[
P=\frac{F}{A}.
\]

Because the pressure comes from the kinetic energy of the gas molecules, a hotter (more energetic) gas produces a larger pressure.

### Doing work on the piston

When the pressure inside the cylinder exceeds the external pressure that pushes on the other side of the piston, the net force on the piston is forward.  
The piston accelerates, moves a small distance \(dx\), and the gas does **work** on it:

\[
dW = F\,dx = P\,A\,dx = P\,dV,
\]

where \(dV = A\,dx\) is the change in the gas’s volume.  

So the gas does mechanical work equal to the product of its pressure and the volume change.  

### Where does that energy come from?

The work \(W\) taken away from the gas is taken from the gas’s **internal energy** \(U\).  
For an ideal gas the internal energy is essentially the sum of the kinetic energies of all its molecules:

\[
U = \frac{3}{2} nRT \qquad (\text{for a monatomic ideal gas}),
\]

where \(n\) is the number of moles, \(R\) the gas constant, and \(T\) the temperature.  

When the gas expands and pushes the piston, some of the molecules transfer part of their kinetic energy to the piston during collisions. The piston’s kinetic energy (and eventually its potential energy if it lifts a weight) grows at the expense of the gas’s internal energy, causing the gas temperature to drop unless heat is supplied from elsewhere.

### Summary

1. **Molecular collisions** with the piston create a pressure.  
2. **Net pressure** greater than the external pressure produces a force that moves the piston.  
3. **Work** done on the piston (\(P\,\Delta V\)) is energy transferred from the gas.  
4. This energy comes from the **kinetic (internal) energy of the gas particles**, so the gas cools as it expands unless heat is added.

Thus the macroscopic motion of the piston is a direct consequence of the microscopic kinetic energy of the gas molecules being transferred, through countless collisions, into mechanical energy of the piston.
rationale: The candidate correctly explains that the piston moves due to energy transfer from gas molecules' kinetic energy via collisions, pressure, and work, consistent with the reference.

**What pushes the piston?**  
Inside the cylinder the gas consists of a huge number of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that move around at high speeds. Every time one of these particles hits the inner wall of the cylinder it bounces off. In the bounce it transfers a little bit of its momentum to the wall.  

If we look at a very small area of the wall, the *average* of all those tiny momentum changes per unit time is what we call **pressure**.  
\[
P=\frac{\text{average force on the wall}}{\text{area of the wall}}
\]

Because the wall is attached to the piston, the same pressure acts on the piston. The piston feels a net outward force  

\[
F = P\,A
\]

where \(A\) is the piston’s cross‑sectional area. As long as this force is larger than any opposing force (the weight of the piston, friction, external pressure, etc.), the piston accelerates and begins to move outward.

---

### From particle energy to piston motion

1. **Particle collisions create pressure**  
   Each collision changes the particle’s direction, but the *speed* (and thus kinetic energy) of the particle is almost unchanged if the wall is rigid. The change in momentum of the particle is transferred to the wall, creating a force.

2. **Work is done when the piston moves**  
   When the piston moves a tiny distance \(dx\), the force \(F\) does an amount of work  

   \[
   dW = F\,dx = P\,A\,dx = P\,dV,
   \]

   where \(dV = A\,dx\) is the small increase in the gas’s volume.

3. **Energy transfer**  
   The work \(dW\) is taken from the *internal energy* of the gas. On a microscopic level, a few of the gas particles lose a little kinetic energy in each collision that pushes the piston outward. The average kinetic energy per particle (which we measure as temperature) therefore drops when the gas expands *without* receiving heat from outside.

4. **Resulting motion of the piston**  
   The piston gains kinetic energy equal to the work done on it:

   \[
   \frac12 M v^2 = \int P\,dV ,
   \]

   where \(M\) is the piston's mass and \(v\) its speed. If the piston eventually comes to rest (e.g., it collides with a stop or encounters an opposing pressure), that kinetic energy is transferred to whatever the piston does next—lifting a weight, heating the surroundings, etc.

---

### Putting it together

- **Microscopic picture:** Fast‑moving gas particles constantly bounce off the piston, each bounce giving the piston a tiny push.
- **Macroscopic picture:** Those countless tiny pushes add up to a pressure. The pressure exerts a net force on the piston, doing work as the piston moves.
- **Energy bookkeeping:** The work done on the piston comes from the gas’s internal (thermal) energy. As the gas expands, its temperature falls if no heat is added, because energy has been transferred to the piston’s motion.

So the piston moves because the kinetic energy of the gas particles, through repeated collisions, produces a pressure that exerts a force on the piston and does mechanical work on it. The gas loses internal energy, while the piston gains kinetic (and eventually other) forms of energy.
rationale: The candidate correctly explains that gas particles' kinetic energy is transferred to the piston via collisions, creating pressure and doing work, which matches the reference.

   A rubber band is a spring‑like material. When you twist it, you put it under torsional strain. The amount of energy \(E\) stored is roughly  

\[

\]

where  

* \(k\) = torsional spring constant of the band (how “stiff” it is)  
* \(\theta\) = angle through which you twist it (how many turns).

Doubling the number of turns roughly quadruples the stored energy because \(\theta\) is squared.

2. **Greater torque on the drive axle**  
   Torque \(\tau\) (the twisting force that makes the wheels turn) is  

\[
\tau = k\,\theta .
\]

A larger \(\theta\) therefore gives a larger torque, so the axle tries to spin faster when you let go.

3. **Higher initial speed**  
   When the band begins to unwind, its stored energy is turned into kinetic energy of the car (both translational motion of the chassis and rotational motion of the wheels). Because more energy is available, the car can reach a higher peak speed, at least for a short time.

4. **Longer run‑time (distance) – up to a point**  
   As the band unwinds, the torque gradually decreases (the band relaxes, \(\theta\) gets smaller). Starting with a larger \(\theta\) means the torque stays positive for a longer portion of the unwind, so the car can keep moving for a longer distance before the band is fully relaxed.

---

### Why the effect isn’t unlimited

| Factor | What it does | Result for the car |
|--------|--------------|--------------------|
| **Friction (wheel bearings, axle, ground)** | Turns some of the rubber‑band energy into heat instead of motion. | A larger torque can overcome friction more easily, but if the torque gets too high the wheels may slip, wasting energy. |
| **Elastic limit of the rubber** | If you twist beyond the band’s elastic region, it will start to deform permanently or break. | The car may stop abruptly or the band may snap, ending the run. |
| **Heat buildup** | Rapid unwinding makes the rubber warm, reducing its stiffness (lower \(k\)). | The later part of the run may be slower than expected. |
| **Mass of the car** | A heavier car needs more energy to accelerate. | Even with a tighter wind, a very heavy car may not gain much extra speed. |

Because of these limits, the improvement from winding tighter is **diminishing**. A modest extra turn usually gives a noticeable speed boost and longer run, but adding many more turns eventually yields only small gains or may cause the band to slip or break.

---

### Bottom line for your rubber‑band car

- **Tighter winding = more stored energy = higher initial speed and a longer distance**, as long as the band stays within its elastic range and the wheels can grip the surface.
- If you wind it **too tightly**, you risk:
  * the band snapping,
  * the wheels spinning without traction,
  * rapid heating that reduces the band’s effectiveness.

**What pushes the piston? – Collisions of the gas molecules**

Inside the cylinder the gas is made of countless tiny particles that move around at high speed.  
When a particle hits the inner face of the piston it bounces back. In that bounce two things happen:

1. **Momentum is transferred.**  
   Momentum is “mass × velocity”. If a particle with mass *m* and speed *v* hits the piston and reverses direction, its momentum changes by about 2 *m v*. By Newton’s third law the piston receives an equal and opposite change of momentum. Repeated hits from many molecules create a steady push on the piston.

2. **Energy is transferred.**  
   The kinetic energy of a particle is \( \tfrac12 m v^{2} \). When it rebounds, part of that kinetic energy is given to the piston (making the piston move) and part stays with the molecule. On average the piston gains a tiny bit of kinetic energy each time a molecule strikes it.

Because there are **huge numbers of molecules** (about \(10^{23}\) in a gram‑scale sample), the continual stream of tiny pushes adds up to a measurable force on the piston.

---

### From many tiny pushes to a macroscopic pressure

The collective effect of all those collisions is described by the gas **pressure** \(P\). Pressure is defined as force per unit area:

\[
P = \frac{\text{total force on the piston}}{\text{area of the piston}}.
\]

If the piston has area \(A\), the total outward force is \(F = P\,A\). As long as the gas stays at the same temperature (i.e., the average kinetic energy of the molecules stays the same), the pressure remains roughly constant.

---

### Doing work on the piston

When the piston moves outward by a small distance \(dx\), the gas does **mechanical work** on it:

\[
\text{d}W = F\,dx = P\,A\,dx = P\,dV,
\]

where \(dV = A\,dx\) is the increase in the gas volume. The total work done while the piston moves from volume \(V_i\) to \(V_f\) is

\[
W = \int_{V_i}^{V_f} P\,dV .
\]

This work comes from the **internal energy** of the gas—the sum of the kinetic energies of all its molecules. In an isolated (adiabatic) expansion no heat enters, so the gas’s internal energy must decrease by exactly the amount of work it does:

\[
\Delta U = -W .
\]

Because the average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to temperature \((\tfrac32 k_{\rm B}T\) for an ideal gas), the gas cools slightly as it pushes the piston outward.

---

### Where does the piston’s energy end up?

The piston’s kinetic energy (or, if it lifts a weight, its gravitational potential energy) comes directly from the gas’s internal energy. Energy is conserved:

\[
\underbrace{U_{\text{initial}}}_{\text{gas}} = 
\underbrace{U_{\text{final}}}_{\text{gas}} +
\underbrace{K_{\text{piston}}}_{\text{motion}} +
\underbrace{U_{\text{piston, grav}}}_{\text{if lifted}} .
\]

If the piston later stops (e.g., hits a stop or is slowed by friction), that mechanical energy can be turned into heat again, raising the temperature of the piston or the surrounding walls.

---

### Quick summary

* The fast‑moving gas molecules constantly collide with the piston, transferring momentum and a tiny amount of kinetic energy each hit.  
* The sum of all those collisions creates a pressure \(P\) that exerts a force \(F = PA\) on the piston.  
* As the piston moves, the gas does work \(W = \int P\,dV\) on it.  
* That work comes from the gas’s internal energy, so the gas cools (its molecules lose a bit of kinetic energy).  
* The piston’s kinetic (or potential) energy is exactly the amount of internal‑energy loss, keeping the total energy conserved.  

In short, the “energy of the gas particles” is transferred through countless molecular collisions, turning microscopic kinetic energy into the macroscopic motion of the piston.

**What changes when you use a bigger solar panel?**  

A solar panel converts sunlight into electrical power (watts). The power it can deliver is roughly

\[
\text{Power (W)} \;=\; \text{solar‑energy per unit area (W m⁻²)} \times \text{panel area (m²)} \times \text{panel efficiency}.
\]

### How the pump responds to more power
